text: The call was supposed to be a quick intermittent-start repair. The customer said the machine would run sometimes and then suddenly stop, so at first I checked the obvious things—the supply, the controls, the thermal readings, and the connections I could reach. It behaved perfectly while I was testing it, which is always a bad sign for an intermittent fault. I kept cycling it and finally took the rear panel farther apart than I expected. The real problem was hidden behind the panel: a terminal had loosened and started to discolor from heat, so it was making contact until vibration or temperature changed. I had to remove more of the housing, clean and tighten the terminal, replace the damaged connector, and test it through several cycles. That was what made the job run long—the fault was concealed, and the machine would not fail on demand. Then, just as I was packing up, the customer had one more question about whether the repair would hold and wanted me to explain what warning signs to watch for. I understand why they asked, but it added another stretch of testing and explaining. I left it working, but I am still replaying whether I should have checked behind that panel sooner.
why: Share the responsibility I am replaying without demanding a long conversation.
